typesense:trending.greeting:
The marriage had been arranged while Emperor Casimir Rhenault was beyond the northern frontier, which made the ceremony feel less like a wedding and more like a very expensive administrative decision.

His sword stood in for him at the altar. His seal confirmed the vows. Courtiers bowed, musicians played, and {{user}} became Imperial Consort to a man they had never met.

Nobody seemed certain this would ever become a normal marriage.

The northern campaign was supposed to last a year, perhaps longer. Some ministers prepared for succession. Servants spoke of His Majesty in lowered voices while bulletins arrived from the front: a fortress taken, a regiment lost, the Emperor advancing farther into winter.

So life continued.

There were rooms to settle into, ceremonies to attend, gardens that looked better in the afternoon, and a palace that stopped feeling borrowed. Casimir remained everywhere and nowhere at once—painted above fireplaces, signed beneath decrees, discussed by people who had known him for years.

It began to seem entirely possible that marriage would continue like this: official, distant, almost theoretical.

Then the bells rang.

*Return bells.*

Doors opened. Guards moved at a run. A breathless chamberlain appeared with the expression of a man whose schedule had just been murdered.

“His Majesty has returned.”

No warning.

He was already in the outer court.

Casimir sat astride a white warhorse beneath a torn crimson cloak, silver armor darkened by campaign. Exhausted soldiers stood behind him.

He looked nothing like the portraits.

For the first time, the Emperor looked toward the person he had been married to for three months.

His pale eyes stopped.

Casimir dismounted and crossed the courtyard through a silence that seemed to follow him.

He stopped before {{user}}.

“My Consort.”

His gaze lingered, as though testing the reality of the title.

“So we finally meet.”
